'''Stephen Anthony Benton''' (December 1, 1941 – November 9, 2003) was the inventor of the [[rainbow hologram]] (Benton hologram) and a pioneer in medical imaging and fine arts holography. Benton held 14 patents in optical physics and photography, and taught media arts and sciences at [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] (MIT). He was the E. Rudge ('48) and Nancy Allen Professor of Media & Sciences, and the Director for Center for Advanced Visual Studies (CAVS) at MIT.

== Biography ==

=== Early life and education ===
Benton was born in [[San Francisco]] in 1941 and grew up in [[Santa Barbara, California]]. He graduated from [[Santa Barbara High School]] in 1959. Benton first became interested in optics at 11 when he wore a pair of 3-D glasses to view the [[Vincent Price]] movie ''[[House of Wax (1953 film)|House of Wax]]''. He recalled, <nowiki>''There was a realism and a sense of excitement like nothing I had ever felt before. Not only was I amazed, I determined then and there to figure out how it worked''</nowiki>.<ref name=":1">{{Cite news|title = Stephen A. Benton, 61, an Expert Researcher in Holography|url = https://www.nytimes.com/2003/11/14/us/stephen-a-benton-61-an-expert-researcher-in-holography.html|newspaper = The New York Times|date = 2003-11-14|access-date = 2015-08-07|issn = 0362-4331|first = Wolfgang|last = Saxon}}</ref> Benton received his undergraduate degree from [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] in electrical engineering (1963) and worked with Professor [[Harold Eugene Edgerton|Harold "Doc" Edgerton]], a pioneer in [[stroboscopy]]. During his undergraduate career, Benton also worked with [[Edwin H. Land]], the co-founder of [[Polaroid Corporation|Polaroid Corp.]] and inventor of instant photography, in the company's vision research laboratory.<ref>{{Cite web|title = Holography pioneer Stephen Benton dies at 61| date=12 November 2003 |url = http://newsoffice.mit.edu/2003/benton|accessdate = 2015-08-07}}</ref>

Benton received his M.S. in 1964 and his Ph.D. in 1968 in [[applied physics]] at [[Harvard University]].

=== Academic career ===
Source:<ref>{{Cite web|title = Stephen Benton - HoloWiki - A Holography FAQ|url = http://holowiki.nss.rpi.edu/wiki/Stephen_Benton|website = holowiki.nss.rpi.edu|accessdate = 2015-08-07|archive-date = 2016-03-04|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20160304135727/http://holowiki.nss.rpi.edu/wiki/Stephen_Benton|url-status = dead}}</ref>

Benton remained at Harvard University as an assistant professor of applied optics until 1973. From 1980 to 1983, Benton returned to MIT as a visiting scientist in the Laser Research Center.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|title = Stephen Benton {{!}} Lemelson-MIT Program|url = http://lemelson.mit.edu/resources/stephen-benton|website = lemelson.mit.edu|accessdate = 2015-08-07}}</ref> While at MIT, he helped form the Spatial Imaging Research Group in 1982.<ref>{{Cite web|title = MIT Media Lab: Spatial Imaging Group|url = http://www.media.mit.edu/spi/|website = www.media.mit.edu|accessdate = 2015-08-07}}</ref> In 1984, Benton joined the MIT faculty as a founding member of the [[MIT Media Lab]], an interdisciplinary research laboratory at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] devoted to projects at the convergence of technology, multimedia, sciences, art and design.<ref name=":0" /> There, he made a lasting impression on his colleagues. "Steve brought a joy and spirit of inventiveness to all that he did," Charles M. Vest, MIT's president, said in a statement. "He was a gifted teacher, scientist, engineer, and artist who personified the best of MIT."<ref name=":2"/> Dr. Benton was the founding head of the MIT Program in Media Arts & Sciences from 1987 to 1994 and became the director for the [http://act.mit.edu/about-act/history/ Center for Advanced Visual Studies (CAVS)] in 1996. He remained the director of CAVS until his death in 2003.<ref>{{Cite web|title = History - ACT at MIT|url = http://act.mit.edu/about-act/history/|accessdate = 2015-08-07}}</ref>

== Inventions ==

=== White Light Transmission Hologram ===
In 1968, Benton began working on the [[rainbow hologram]] or the Benton hologram, at [[Polaroid Corporation]]. Rainbow holography makes use of common white light to visualize holograms rather than lasers, thereby leading "holography out of the lab".<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2">{{Cite web|title = Boston.com / News / Boston Globe / Obituaries / Stephen Benton; his holograms melded science, art, commerce|url = https://archive.boston.com/news/globe/obituaries/articles/2003/11/14/stephen_benton_his_holograms_melded_science_art_commerce/|website = www.boston.com|access-date = 2015-08-07}}</ref> This type of hologram is commonly seen as the [[dove]] on the [[Visa Inc.|Visa]] card.<ref name=":3">{{Cite web|url = http://www.osa-opn.org/Content/ViewFile.aspx?id=3598|title = In Memory: Stephen Benton|accessdate = 2015-08-07|website = |publisher = Optics & Photonics News|last = Phillips|first = Nicholas}}</ref> The first rainbow hologram, termed "Motif 1," was presented on a 4-by-5-inch glass plate. It consisted of three chess pieces illuminated by a single white light bulb. Dr. Benton first presented his invention to the optical society in California in 1968.<ref name=":2" /> This discovery was also of great interest to the artistic community, as "fiercely bright images which could be manipulated in an artistic context were observed".<ref name=":3" /> Since the rainbow hologram was very easy to mass-produce, today, credit card companies and state agencies widely make use of rainbow holograms to deter counterfeiting of credit cards and identification cards.<ref name=":2" />

His research in holography helped in the advancement of holographic technology integral to medical imaging devices like CT and MRI scanners.<ref name=":1" />

=== Real Image Holographic Stereograms ===
In 1988, Dr. Benton patented methods and devices for projecting and recording holographic [[Stereoscopy|stereograms]]. This invention utilized a semi-cylindrical "alcove" display system in front of which an image is projected. This provides the viewer with a wider angle of view compared to the traditional hologram (180 degrees compared to 30 degrees), allowing viewers to look around most of the image content.<ref>{{Cite web|title = Real image holographic stereograms Patent (Patent # 4,834,476 issued May 30, 1989) - Justia Patents Database|url = http://patents.justia.com/patent/4834476|website = patents.justia.com|accessdate = 2015-08-07}}</ref>

=== Holographic Color Control Systems ===
Benton and his students optimized the production of [[False color|pseudocolor]] holograms, which was patented in 1989. This had implications as a way of rendering three dimensional computer generated designs.<ref>{{Cite web|title = Holographic color control systems Patent (Patent # 4,986,619 issued January 22, 1991) - Justia Patents Database|url = http://patents.justia.com/patent/4986619|website = patents.justia.com|accessdate = 2015-08-07}}</ref>

=== Interactive Holographic Video System ===
In this invention, users are able to interact with and modify an electronic holographic image using a [[Haptic technology|force-feedback]] (or haptic) device. This device can sense, report the position, and display appropriate forces to the user. The user can feel and modify specified shapes in the workspace. The haptic workspace is linked with the free-standing, spatial image displayed by a holographic video (holovideo) system. This interactive workspace allows a user to see, feel, and interact with synthetic objects that feel like real ones. The display allows these objects to become a part of the user's workspace.<ref>{{Cite web|title = Dynamic holographic video with haptic interaction Patent (Patent # 6,211,848 issued April 3, 2001) - Justia Patents Database|url = http://patents.justia.com/patent/6211848|website = patents.justia.com|accessdate = 2015-08-07}}</ref>

== Artwork ==
Not only was Stephen Benton an accomplished scientist, but also an artist. Benton thought of holography as an <nowiki>''intersection of art, science and technology''</nowiki> One of his works, ''Volumetric Rendering of Magnetic Resonance Imaging--Acquired Data'', Digital Hologram is currently on display at [[Brigham and Women's Hospital]].<ref>{{Cite web|title = Digital Holography {{!}} The MIT 150 Exhibition|url = http://museum.mit.edu/150/98|website = museum.mit.edu|accessdate = 2015-08-07}}</ref> His own works in holography have been displayed at the Museum of Holography on Mercer Street in Manhattan, where he was a curator. Currently, MIT holds the entire collection of Benton's holograms as the Museum of Holography went bankrupt in 1992.<ref name=":1" />

== Professional societies and other honors ==
1976 – 1977: President of the New England section of OSA<ref name=":4">{{Cite web|title = Stephen Benton {{!}} In Memoriam {{!}} The Optical Society|url = http://www.osa.org/en-us/about_osa/newsroom/obituaries/stephen_benton/|website = www.osa.org|accessdate = 2015-08-07}}</ref>

1980 – 1984: Chairman for the U.S. National Committee for the International Commission for Optics<ref name=":4" />

1990 – 1993: Board of Directors for the International Society for Optical Engineering (SPIE)<ref name=":4" />

1995: Vinci of Excellence Award at the International Science for Art competition<ref name=":0" />

1999: Vice President for the Society for Imaging Science and Technology<ref name=":4" />

2005: Posthumously awarded the [[Edwin H. Land Medal]]<ref>{{Cite web |date=2005-06-08 |title=Awards and Honors |url=https://news.mit.edu/2005/aandh-0608 |access-date=2024-06-17 |website=MIT News {{!}} Massachusetts Institute of Technology |language=en}}</ref>

Board of Trustees for the Museum of Holography in New York<ref name=":0" />

Boards of Trustees for Rochester's Museum of Photography at Georges Eastman's House<ref name=":0" />

== In popular culture ==
The [[List of Jem characters|Benton family]] from the animated TV series ''[[Jem (TV series)|Jem and The Holograms]]'' was named after the holography pioneer.
